subject: Clarifying pricing metrics: tokens vs characters vs requests (Acme Health)

Subject: Follow-up + pricing metric clarification from today's call

Thanks again for the time today — great discussion on your clinical summarization POC and where latency/cost tradeoffs matter. As promised, a short recap and a couple of clarifying questions so we can model cost accurately: 

1) Quick recap of what we heard you use in the POC:
- Average request: ~1.2–1.5k input tokens (patient notes + prompt) and ~200–400 output tokens (summary).
- Peak concurrency: ~300 req/min, but steady state expected to be ~60–100 req/min.
- Goal: keep latency < 800ms 95th and target $/1M tokens in line with budget.

2) Clarification needed (you mentioned different internal metrics):
- You said Acme typically measures usage in characters rather than tokens — can you confirm an example (e.g., 50k characters/day)?
- Do your product analytics report requests (counts) or raw characters/KB?
- Do you expect prompt caching to reduce billed volume (same patient prompts repeated)?

If you can share a short sample of last 7 days of usage (attach CSV or screenshot) and a rough budget range for inference spend (monthly), we can run some unit-economics scenarios and show $/1M token equivalents for your workflows. 

Next steps I propose:
- You share a 7-day sample (CSV fine) — we'll return 2 scenarios (aggressive caching + no caching) with cost per 1M tokens and monthly projection.
- Optional 30-minute pricing walk-through to align on metrics and conversion.

Thanks — attaching the default pricing sheet for reference.

Thanks, Marissa — this is helpful. Quick answers and a few clarifying points from our side: 

- We currently instrument usage in characters on our analytics side (legacy). Example: last week we saw ~3.6M characters/day across the summarization service. 
- Product analytics also report requests (we average ~80k requests/day; peaks higher).
- Regarding caching: we do a partial prefix cache in prod for repeated templates, but much of the patient text is unique. We expect 10–20% cache hit on identical prompts; more substantial gains if we can cache canonical templates.
- Budget: our initial monthly budget range for inference is between $8k–$20k while we validate quality. Not sure yet what that translates to in $/1M tokens. 

Attached is a CSV export with last 7 days of requests + character counts. Sorry for mixing characters/requests — our analytics team uses characters, model teams use tokens; that's the source of the confusion.

Could you provide an example conversion you use (characters -> tokens) and a worked example for our numbers? Also curious how Redwood treats prompt caching vs billed tokens — do cached responses avoid billing entirely or just reduce average tokens?

—
Alice Turner

alice.turner@acmehealth.com

From: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.ai>
To: Alice Turner <alice.turner@acmehealth.com>, Bob Li <bob.li@acmehealth.com>
Cc: Ethan Park <ethan.park@redwood.ai>
Date: 2026-07-30T12:18:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Follow-up + pricing metric clarification from today's call

Great — thanks for the CSV and the budget range, Alice. Below I've laid out the conversions and a couple of worked examples so your team can map characters/requests -> tokens -> billable units. Hoping this clears the main confusion points. 

Short answers to your direct questions:
- Characters -> tokens: rough heuristic: 4 characters ~= 1 token for English text (this varies by language and punctuation). So 3.6M characters/day ~= ~900k tokens/day (3,600,000 / 4).
- Requests vs tokens: we bill per token processed (input + output). Request counts are useful for concurrency/throughput sizing and per-request overheads but not directly billed.
- Prompt caching: caching can reduce billed tokens when we can serve from an exact cache key (prefix+input). Our platform supports prefix/KV caching — when a cache hit occurs and we serve a stored response, those tokens are not executed on the model and are not billed. Partial caching (e.g., cached prompt prefix but dynamic patient text appended) reduces compute per request only if we can avoid re-generating the cached portion; typically this yields token savings but depends on how the prompt is structured.

Worked examples (using your numbers):
- Example A (no caching): 80k requests/day * average (input 1.4k tokens + output 300 tokens) = 80k * 1700 = 136M tokens/day. At 30 days -> ~4.08B tokens/month.
- Example B (10% cache hit that returns full cached response): 80k requests/day * 1700 tokens * 0.9 = 122.4M tokens/day -> ~3.67B tokens/month.
- Example using characters: 3.6M characters/day -> ~900k tokens/day. If your analytics character numbers represent only input text (and model output is additional), add estimated output tokens (e.g., +300 tokens per request * 80k req/day = 24M tokens/day) — that discrepancy is why characters vs tokens can look so different.

Unit economics (illustrative):
- If we use a $/1M token baseline of $150 (example tier for hosted burst with no committed discounts):
  - 1M tokens costs $150.
  - Example A monthly cost (4.08B tokens) = 4080 * $150 = $612,000/month (obviously far above your stated budget).
  - Example B (3.67B tokens) = 3670 * $150 = $550,500/month.

Clearly those raw numbers don't align with your $8k–$20k budget — this suggests either your character numbers are not equivalent to tokens processed for inference (e.g., analytics counting characters of a different pipeline) or your POC test set is much smaller than full prod. Two levers to get within budget: 
1) Reduce tokens per request (prompt engineering, shorter outputs, summarize progressively).
2) Heavy caching / canonicalization (move as much as possible into templates that can be cached) and/or commit to Dedicated capacity (reserved pricing) which lowers $/1M tokens significantly.

Proposed next steps:
- Our ask: can you confirm whether the 3.6M characters/day is counted pre- or post- truncation and whether it maps to the same traffic hitting the model endpoint?
- I'll run a 3-scenario cost model for you (hosted list pricing, hosted with 25% caching, dedicated reserved capacity estimate) and share a one-page summary with numbers and recommended optimizations.
- If helpful, let's schedule a 30-minute pricing deep-dive tomorrow — Ethan (cc'd) can join to cover Dedicated pricing and commit math.

If you want quicker visibility, we can also ingest your CSV and return a per-day token estimate (we need to map characters -> tokens per row). Happy to do that if you confirm it's okay for us to process the sample.

—
Marissa Cole
Account Executive, Redwood Inference
marissa@redwood.ai
